en: The Nakulasaṃpradājavardhaṇī is praised as excellent when free from defects.

Having bathed them with water and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and having smeared them with perfumes and other substances, the skillful and wise preceptor should worship them; in this regard, everything concerning the tree is to be performed exactly as prescribed.

At the time of entering the city, he should bring within the range of perception of the king and the citizens the auspicious news from the forest regarding the king of trees, the mountain, and the rock fragments.

The Guru, who is a mantra-master of the Jina, should have [the image] carried away by people whose hearts are full of joy and who are intoxicated with passion, amidst the sounds of musical instruments and songs;
having placed a jar filled with curd and water at the entrance.
He is to be worshipped by beautiful women with their intoxicating side-glances.
Having been ushered in by his circle of kinsmen, whose hearts were filled with supreme joy, with showers of garments, flower-garlands, perfumes, lamps, and water,
he was placed upon a vast, level, and auspicious ground in the midst of a lotus made of flour.
One should place it, sprinkled with water from the Guru's hand, for the sake of accomplishing the ritual action. 〔Spiral〕 ॥
The seventh chapter: On the Forest Expedition. [70] The incomparable and auspicious characteristics, including the measurements of the site and so forth, have been fully prescribed.
This was taught by the Buddhas, whose minds are filled with compassion, in various sections of their own scriptures.
From the conjunction of seven *paramāṇus* comes what is called an *aṇu*; from seven *aṇus*, a *sūkṣmarajas* (subtle dust);
and from seven *rajas* particles, that which is designated by the wise as an *iṭakarajas* (dust mote).
Seven of these particles of dust make one "cow-dust" (*gauraja*), and seven of those make one louse (*yūkā*);
thus the calculation proceeds, with seven lice making one barley-corn (*yava*).
A finger-measure (*aṅgulikā*) consists of seven barley grains; the middle [finger] consists of eight barley grains;
and the smallest, known as *kanyasī*, consists of six barley grains—these are the auspicious ones.
By doubling those twelve *vārṣtis*, a *hasta* shall be formed;
indeed, there are three kinds of *hastas*—the smallest, the middle, and the largest—according to the distinction of the [four] castes (*varṇa*).

Those whose fingers and hands are disproportionate, yet who are auspicious and capable of performing all tasks, should be avoided by those seeking their own welfare in these undertakings; rather, those who are symmetrical [should be chosen].
The banner, smoke, lion, dog, bull, donkey, elephant, crow, and blue jay— these eight, when combined with the [planetary] lords as determined by experts, should be employed in all undertakings.

This banner is highly praised for ascetics and brahmins who desire the protection of sacred narratives; it is likewise for the lion-like Kṣatriya kings who long for the heroic power to conquer the earth.

The bull is for the Śūdra people who desire the nourishment and increase of wealth and grain; the elephant is for the Vaiśya merchants who desire mastery over cattle, dependents, and prosperity. || [curl] ||
